strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem: universal, transferable, black-box patch attacks on VLA-driven robots, which has direct safety relevance for embodied AI deployment.

The framework is technically comprehensive, combining a feature-space L1/contrastive objective, a robustness-augmented (min-max) patch optimization inspired by adversarially-trained surrogate transfer literature, and two novel VLA-specific losses (Patch Attention Dominance and Patch Semantic Misalignment) that target cross-modal attention and instruction grounding rather than only pixel-level perturbation.

The paper provides a theoretical motivation (Assumption 1, Proposition 1, Corollary 1) linking surrogate-side feature deviations to target-side deviations, giving some principled justification for the design choices, and supports it empirically with CCA/linear-probe evidence of shared representational structure.

Thorough ablation studies (Table 3, Table 4) isolate the contribution of each loss term (RUPA, PAD, PSM, Jtr components) and text-probe design, showing that most components contribute non-trivially to transfer performance.

Qualitative patch analysis (Fig. 2) shows the proposed patches avoid surrogate/embodiment-specific textures (e.g., gripper mimicry) seen in baseline methods, supporting the claim of more model-agnostic, transferable perturbations.

Evaluation spans multiple task suites (LIBERO Spatial/Object/Goal/Long) and multiple victim models (OpenVLA-oft variants, OpenVLA-oft-w, mention of π0), providing reasonably broad coverage for the black-box transfer claims made in the main text.
weaknesses: Numerous appendix references are broken ("Appendix ??") throughout the paper, meaning several claims central to the paper's argument—white-box performance, transfer results to π0 (the most architecturally distinct victim and the strongest test of the universality claim), and even the proof of Proposition 1—are asserted but not verifiable in the submitted manuscript.

The distinction between "Simulated" and "Physical" columns in Tables 1-2 is unclear and potentially misleading: both appear to report LIBERO (simulator) success rates against different training-data checkpoints (LIBERO-Long-trained vs. BridgeData V2-trained models) rather than actual physical robot trials, despite the title ("When Robots Obey the Patch") and abstract explicitly claiming "physical executions" and real-world validation. This terminology should be clarified or the physical-world claims should be tempered.

The linear-alignment assumption (Assumption 1) underlying the theoretical justification is a strong simplification of the relationship between very different VLA architectures (e.g., autoregressive OpenVLA vs. flow-based π-series), and the supporting empirical evidence (a single R²≈0.654 value) is reported without sufficient methodological detail (which layers, which model pair, which data) to assess its generality.

The reported effectiveness of the proposed method varies substantially across victim/setting combinations (e.g., near-complete task failure in Table 1 simulated at 5.75% average success vs. only moderate degradation to 61.5% in Table 2 physical), which somewhat undercuts the "universal" framing and is not thoroughly discussed or explained beyond noting a "larger distribution and policy gap."

No defense or countermeasure evaluation is provided despite the paper positioning itself as "establishing a strong baseline for future defenses"; without at least a basic defense/detection baseline, this claim is unsupported by evidence in the manuscript.

Baseline comparison is limited to a single prior work's six objective variants (RoboticAttack); broader comparison with other transfer-based or feature-space adversarial patch methods from the general (non-VLA) adversarial robustness literature discussed in Related Work is absent, limiting the strength of the comparative claims.

Implementation details necessary for reproducibility (patch size/area budget, hyperparameters α, β, λ weights, number of probe phrases, training schedule) are deferred to the missing appendix, making it difficult to assess or reproduce the method from the main text alone.

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored gap: most prior VLA adversarial-patch work assumes white-box access to a single victim, while this paper targets universal, transferable, black-box patch attacks with a systematic framework (UPA-RFAS).

The methodology combines multiple well-motivated components tailored to VLA architecture: a feature-space l1+contrastive objective grounded in a linear-alignment assumption with a supporting proposition/corollary, a robustness-augmented bi-level (inner PGD / outer patch) optimization inspired by robust-surrogate transfer literature, and two VLA-specific losses (attention hijacking and semantic misalignment) that go beyond generic feature attacks.
Reasonably thorough ablations isolating the contribution of each loss term, patch size, contrastive weight, and the inner perturbation budget, which helps interpret the design choices.

Qualitative real-world robot demonstrations and patch-pattern visualizations (Fig. 2) that contrast the proposed feature-space patch against baseline object-mimicking patches, offering some intuition for why the method transfers better.
The paper reports both white-box and black-box results and includes cross-family transfer to a structurally different VLA (π0), which is a meaningful and difficult transfer setting.
weaknesses: The central theoretical justification (Assumption 1: linear alignment between surrogate and target feature spaces) is only loosely validated by a single R²≈0.654 regression-probe number and unspecified residual bound εE; this is a fairly weak empirical basis for a claim underpinning the entire framework's transferability guarantee, and no evidence is given that this assumption holds across the diverse victim models actually tested.

The 'universal transferable' claim is only strongly supported for OpenVLA→OpenVLA-oft transfer, which is a fine-tuned variant of the same base architecture rather than a genuinely different model family; transfer to the structurally distinct π0 model (Table 5) shows only modest degradation (e.g., 92%→86% simulated, 92%→83.5% physical), which is far less convincing evidence of true architecture-agnostic universality than the headline numbers suggest.

The experimental setup description for 'Simulated' vs 'Physical' settings in Table 1 is confusing: it is unclear how a model trained on real-world BridgeData v2 is evaluated on LIBERO spatial/object/goal/long task suites, since these are simulation-specific tasks; this ambiguity makes it hard to verify what is actually being measured as 'physical' performance and raises concerns about experimental rigor/clarity.
Real-world physical validation is purely qualitative (3 trials × 3 tasks, no quantitative success-rate statistics), which is insufficient to substantiate claims of practical real-world threat.

In the white-box setting (Table 4/Appendix C), several baseline objectives (e.g., UADA1−3) achieve equal or stronger attack success than the proposed method, which is only briefly acknowledged; this partially undercuts the narrative that the proposed objective is uniformly superior.

Ablations and analysis are conducted almost exclusively against a single victim (OpenVLA-oft); it is unclear whether the same component-wise conclusions (e.g., importance of PAD/PSM/RUPA) hold for the more distant π0 victim, limiting confidence in the generality of the design choices.
The paper does not compare against or discuss any adversarial-patch defenses or provide guidance on detectability, despite claiming to establish 'a baseline for future defenses.'

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem: universal, transferable, black-box patch attacks on VLA-driven robots, which is more practically relevant than the white-box patch attacks studied in prior work (e.g., RoboticAttack).

The framework is well-motivated by an explicit theoretical link (Assumption 1, Proposition 1, Corollary 1) between surrogate-side and target-side feature deviations, giving a principled justification for the ℓ1 deviation objective, supported empirically with CCA and linear-probe R^2 analysis.

The design combines complementary signals (feature-space ℓ1+contrastive, attention hijacking via PAD, semantic misalignment via PSM, and a robustness-augmented bi-level optimization) that are individually motivated and empirically validated via ablation (Table 2), showing each component contributes to transfer.

Extensive empirical evaluation across multiple victim architectures with different fine-tuning recipes (OpenVLA-oft, OpenVLA-oft-w) and a structurally different backbone (π0), across both simulated and 'physical'-trained models, and across four LIBERO task suites, demonstrating consistently stronger black-box degradation than several strong baselines.

Useful auxiliary analyses: patch-size sensitivity, hyperparameter ablations (λcon, ϵ in RUPA), text-probe phrasing ablation, and qualitative patch-pattern comparison showing the proposed patch avoids object/embodiment-specific mimicry unlike baselines.
Includes a qualitative real-robot demonstration in addition to simulated/dataset-based evaluation, showing some evidence of practical applicability beyond simulation.
weaknesses: The distinction between 'Simulated' and 'Physical' settings in the main quantitative tables (e.g., Table 1) is not clearly defined in the main text — it appears 'Physical' refers to a model trained on real-world BridgeData V2 but still evaluated via rollouts rather than an actual robot, which is confusingly different from the qualitative real-world trials in Appendix F (only 3 tasks x 3 trials, no baseline comparison, no quantitative success rate). This blurs the paper's central claim of 'physical execution' transfer.

The theoretical justification (Assumption 1, linear alignment) is only moderately supported empirically: R^2 ≈ 0.654 for the linear probe is not particularly high, meaning a substantial portion of target-side feature variance is not explained by the assumed linear map, which weakens the rigor of the transferability guarantee built on top of it.

All surrogate experiments use only OpenVLA-derived models (OpenVLA-7B and its LIBERO-Long variant); the paper never demonstrates surrogate diversity (e.g., a non-OpenVLA surrogate), so claims of general 'model-agnostic' transfer rest entirely on the victim side, leaving open whether the specific surrogate family biases the learned universal directions.

No comparison to or discussion of applying existing defenses (adversarial training on VLAs, patch detection/removal, smoothing) despite the paper positioning itself as 'a baseline for future defenses'; this limits the completeness of the security assessment.

The code repository link is left blank/placeholder, and given the complexity of the pipeline (bi-level optimization, attention/semantic loss computation across model-specific internals), reproducibility relies heavily on the released code that is not verifiably available at submission time.

Patch size used in main results (5%, with an ablation up to 10%) is relatively large and visually conspicuous for a 'patch' attack, raising questions about stealthiness/practicality claims relative to smaller, more classically 'patch-like' adversarial perturbations.

Table 1 (the main transfer results) lacks variance/standard deviation across trials, unlike Tables 4 and 5, making it harder to assess the statistical reliability of the reported success-rate drops, especially for close comparisons (e.g., ablation differences of a few percentage points in Table 2).
